introduction.text: Monte Testaccio is an artificial mound in Rome made almost entirely of broken olive oil amphorae. It is one of the largest spoil heaps in the ancient world and provides a unique record of Rome's imperial oil trade and state distribution system.

history.description: Monte Testaccio was constructed as a structured waste disposal for olive oil amphorae, with terraces and retaining walls, and was used from around AD 140 to 250.
At its peak, Rome imported up to 130,000 amphorae per year, representing about 7.5 million liters of olive oil annually.
Dumping of amphorae ceased after about the 260s.
In 1849, the hill was used as a gun battery under Giuseppe Garibaldi during the defence of Rome.
The first archaeological investigation began in 1872 by Heinrich Dressel, with further work in the 1980s and 1994.
The hill was used on Good Friday to represent Golgotha during papal processions.

design.description: The mound consists of a series of level terraces with retaining walls made of intact amphorae filled with sherds, and lime was sprinkled over the broken pots.
